title: Does your school have the same teacher to student ratio?
description: The ratio of five teachers to one hundred seventy students is reduced to the simplest form. A sample school is then reduced the same way and the two simplest forms are compared.
teaching_notes: One idea: two schools match only if their ratios have the same simplest form. Watch for students who compare only the number of teachers.

source: Example (teachers and students in your school)
video_script.why: The child compares two real-life ratios by reducing both to the simplest form.
video_script.substitution: Write teachers to students for each school, reduce both by the highest common factor, and compare.
video_script.anchor: two school cards: the book's school with 5 teachers and 170 students, and a sample school with 12 teachers and 360 students
video_script.payoff_line: A school matches only if its ratio also reduces to one to thirty four.

final_answer.value: 5 : 170 is 1 : 34; your school's ratio is proportional only if it also reduces to 1 : 34
final_answer.spoken: five to one hundred seventy is one to thirty four, and a school matches only if its ratio also reduces to one to thirty four

maths_rules: sample school used to show the method (the book asks the child to count their own school): 12 teachers and 360 students, so 12 : 360
1 : 30 is not 1 : 34, so the sample school does not match; it has fewer students for each teacher
video_script.design: One idea: reduce both school ratios and compare the simplest forms. Uses the simplest form test of the solved example. The two school cards stay for the whole video.
open_questions: The book asks the child to count their own school, so the video shows the method on a sample school of 12 teachers and 360 students. These numbers are not in the book.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a school.
<bookmark mark='sch'/>The school has five teachers and one hundred seventy students.
<bookmark mark='own'/>You count the teachers and the students in your own school.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Does your school have the same ratio of teachers to students?

beats.on_screen: the two cards hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: teachers : students written for two schools; each reduced by ÷ highest common factor to its simplest form; the two simplest forms placed side by side

marks.same: the two school cards line up
marks.simple: an arrow ÷ highest common factor gives each ratio in the words simplest form
marks.cmp: the two simplest forms are placed side by side to compare

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='simple'/>Divide both terms by their highest common factor. The ratio we get is called its simplest form.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>Two schools match only if their simplest forms are the same.

beats.on_screen: Given: the school has 5 teachers and 170 students; for example, your school has 12 teachers and 360 students

marks.a: the book's school numbers are written
marks.b: for example, 12 teachers and 360 students is written for your school

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Given, the school has five teachers and one hundred seventy students.
<bookmark mark='b'/>Say your school has twelve teachers and three hundred sixty students, as an example.

beats.on_screen: To find: whether the two schools have the same teachers : students ratio

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether the two schools have the same ratio of teachers to students.

marks.d: 5 ÷ 5 = 1 and 170 ÷ 5 = 34 are written and 1 : 34 is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='r'/>Step one, the book's school has the ratio five to one hundred seventy. The highest common factor is five.
<bookmark mark='d'/>Dividing both terms by five gives one to thirty four.

marks.t: 12 is written first for the teachers
marks.s: 360 is written second for the students

narration: <bookmark mark='t'/>Step two, in the example school, write the teachers first, which is twelve.
<bookmark mark='s'/>Then write the students, which is three hundred sixty.
<bookmark mark='r'/>The ratio is twelve to three hundred sixty.

marks.h: HCF of 12 and 360 is 12 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='h'/>Step three, the highest common factor of twelve and three hundred sixty is twelve.
<bookmark mark='d'/>Twelve divided by twelve is one, and three hundred sixty divided by twelve is thirty.
<bookmark mark='s'/>The simplest form is one to thirty.

beats.on_screen: 1 : 30 is not 1 : 34; the example school has fewer students for each teacher. Check: 5 × 34 = 170 and 12 × 30 = 360

marks.cmp: 1 : 30 and 1 : 34 are placed side by side
marks.chk: the words Check: 5 × 34 = 170 and 12 × 30 = 360 are written and ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step four, compare one to thirty with one to thirty four.
<bookmark mark='no'/>They are not the same, so the example school does not match. It has fewer students for each teacher.
<bookmark mark='chk'/>Check by multiplying back. Five times thirty four is one hundred seventy, and twelve times thirty is three hundred sixty.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 5 : 170 is 1 : 34; your school's ratio is proportional only if it also reduces to 1 : 34
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Five to one hundred seventy is one to thirty four. A school matches only if its ratio also reduces to one to thirty four.
